title: From accidents to assets—The value pathways of patents for serendipitous inventions
authors: Christoph Grimpe; Karin Hoisl; Myriam Mariani; Wolfgang Sofka
affiliations: Department of Strategy and Innovation Copenhagen Business School Frederiksberg Denmark; Mannheim Business School University of Mannheim Mannheim Germany; Max Planck Institute for Innovation and Competition Munich Germany; Department of Management and Technology and ICRIOS Bocconi University Milan Italy; Strategy, International Business and Entrepreneurship Group (SIBE) University of Liverpool Management School Liverpool UK
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Firms often celebrate accidental inventions that lead to major breakthroughs, yet little is known about how the value of serendipitous inventions materializes. Using data from 8530 patented inventions across 23 countries, our research shows that these inventions differ from planned R&D outcomes. Serendipitous inventions are less likely to have a strong technological impact, be turned into marketable products, or serve as effective blocking tools in patent strategy. However, they are more likely to generate value through licensing, indicating that while they may not fit the originating firm's strategy, they can succeed elsewhere. Hence, serendipitous patented inventions represent “option‐like” assets that offer external channels to capture value rather than relying on internal use. Managerial Summary Accidental breakthroughs like microwaves, penicillin, or Velcro are often celebrated, but their potential to create value in practice remains unclear. Analyzing data from 8530 patented inventions across 23 countries, we find that such serendipitous inventions differ fundamentally from planned R&D outcomes. They are less likely to yield major technological impacts, products, or strategic patents but more likely to generate value through licensing, functioning as “option‐like” assets that are valuable externally more than internally. Thus, relative to planned inventions that benefit from downstream complementary assets, serendipitous patented inventions pay off more for firms with strong licensing or technology‐selling capabilities.

title: Accommodation in the vertical supply chain: Implications of manufacturer dual tracking
authors: Young Hou
affiliations: Strategy, Ethics & Entrepreneurship University of Virginia Darden School of Business Charlottesville Virginia USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary The prevalence of dual tracking, in which upstream manufacturers simultaneously produce branded and private‐label products for downstream retailers, has increased substantially in recent years, driven by growing consumer demand for private‐label products. This paper examines the implications of manufacturer dual tracking by exploiting a setting in the ready‐to‐eat breakfast cereal industry where a leading branded manufacturer began supplying both products to retailers. We find that, because of this change in the vertical relationship, private‐label product introductions and advertising declined for products that directly imitated the dual‐tracking manufacturer's branded products. Changes in retailer behavior suggest that retailers accommodated the dual‐tracking manufacturer by selectively adjusting their private‐label portfolios. Dual tracking can therefore improve a manufacturer's bargaining position against retailers and reduce downstream imitation. Managerial Summary Manufacturers have increasingly produced not only their own branded products but also private‐label products for retailers that compete with those brands. This phenomenon, known as dual tracking, carries benefits and risks for manufacturers. While producing private‐label products can utilize excess capacity, these products directly compete with the branded counterpart. We study the implications for firms engaging in dual tracking and show that doing so gives manufacturers greater bargaining power in their relationships with retailers. Firms can leverage this change in bargaining power to reduce imitation by retailers' private‐label products, lessening competition concerns. Our results show that retailers reduced the introduction and advertising of private‐label products that directly compete with the dual‐tracking manufacturer.

title:
Managing Collaboration Dynamics Under Pressure: Lessons From the
                    <scp>COVID</scp>
                    ‐19 Medical Supply Shortage
authors: Christopher Bowers; Qian Hu; James L. Olds
affiliations: US Department of Defense Washington DC USA; Schar School of Policy and Government George Mason University Washington DC USA
abstract: ABSTRACT In crisis responses such as the COVID‐19 medical supply shortage, senior policy makers often emphasize urgency, a strategy that prioritizes the rapid achievement of intermediate goals. While this approach can drive swift action, it also introduces challenges and trade‐offs that can hinder collaboration toward long‐term success. These challenges often arise from misalignment between organizational norms and priorities of collaborating partners, which can undermine legitimacy and performance. Policymakers should consider how personnel composition, such as large military contingents, shapes task force culture and operational dynamics. Even in fast‐moving crises, clearly aligning roles, goals, and timelines from the start can reduce confusion, while leaders must navigate cultural norms and challenge ingrained practices to support collaboration.

title: Erratum: “Dynamic Pricing and Matching for Two-Sided Queues”
authors: Sushil Mahavir Varma; Pornpawee Bumpensanti; Siva Theja Maguluri; He Wang
affiliations: School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30332; Amazon, Bellevue, Washington 98004
abstract: Corrections to the Publication “Dynamic Pricing and Matching for Two-Sided Queues” In the context of two-sided queues, Theorem 2 of the paper [Dynamic Pricing and Matching for Two-Sided Queues. Operations Research 2023;71(1):83–100] establishes optimality guarantees for the two-price policy combined with the max-weight matching policies. As stated, this theorem is not valid. In this erratum, we show that the conclusions of Theorem 2 hold under a slight modification of the max-weight policy, which does not use some of the edges in the graph to match. Moreover, we point out some technical issues in this paper and outline how to resolve them.

title: Social Networks as Information Conduits for Online Credit Supply and Demand
authors: Linda Allen; Lin Peng; Yu Shan
affiliations: Zicklin School of Business, Baruch College/CUNY, New York, New York 10010; Whitman School of Management, Syracuse University, Syracuse, New York 13244
abstract: We study how intercommunity social networks influence loan demand and supply on fintech lending platforms. Demand for online loans rises following increases in online borrowing activity in geographically distant but socially connected areas. On the supply side, borrower area social proximity to deposit-rich regions increases funding likelihood and is associated with better ex post loan performance. We establish causality with shift-share instrumental variables (SSIVs) obtained from natural disasters (demand side) and financial adviser misconduct (supply side). Social connectedness expands both loan demand and supply in disadvantaged communities without increasing delinquency rates. Intercommunity social networks raise awareness of alternative lending platforms and transmit hard-to-obtain information that mitigates community-level information asymmetry. This paper has been accepted by Will Cong for the Virtual Special Issue on Digital Finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06050 .

title: Improving Competitiveness: A Freelancer-Centric Approach for Recommending Reskilling Strategies
authors: Haoxin Liu; Shuo Yu; Stephen He; Wen Wen; Yidong Chai
affiliations: Hefei University of Technology, Department of Electronic Commerce, Hefei, Anhui, China; Texas Tech University Rawls College of Business, Area of Information Systems and Quantitative Sciences, Lubbock, Texas, United States; The University of Texas at San Antonio, Marketing, San Antonio, Texas, 78249-1644, United States; The University of Texas at Austin, McCombs School of Business, Austin, Texas, United States
abstract: Online labor markets play a vital role in connecting freelancers and employers worldwide. While most existing methods focus on helping employers find the best candidates, relatively little research addresses freelancer-centric approaches. In this study, we propose a freelancer-centric skill advisor (FESA) that combines a competitiveness evaluator and an optimization model. The competitiveness evaluator integrates a state-of-the-art deep learning recommender system with contrastive learning to calculate matching scores between freelancers and their desired tasks, while the optimization model prescribes skills a freelancer should acquire to improve their competitiveness for those tasks while making the learning experience manageable. FESA also supports two reskilling strategies: exploration and exploitation. We evaluate FESA against alternative recommendation models using a large-scale, real-world dataset collected from a leading online labor market. We also conduct a controlled experiment with human participants to examine how real-world users respond to FESA recommendations and whether disclosing a freelancer’s ranking, a key output of FESA, affects reskilling motivation. In contrast to prior findings from traditional organizational settings, where ranking information generally encourages greater effort, we find that disclosing a freelancer’s low ranking significantly reduces motivation to reskill. This demotivating effect of ranking disclosure is more pronounced under the exploration reskilling strategy, which requires freelancers to acquire more challenging and unfamiliar skills, than under the exploitation reskilling strategy where freelancers are advised to acquire skills that are more closely aligned with their existing expertise. Our research highlights that designing a freelancer-centric recommendation system requires not only algorithmic innovation but also careful attention of how system design influences user motivation and engagement.

title: From Data-Model Fit to Model-World Fit: A Framework for Integrating Domain Knowledge into Artificial Intelligence
authors: Arturo Castellano; Monica Chiarini Tremblay; Roman Lukyanenko; Jeffrey Parsons; Veda C. Storey
affiliations: College of William & Mary, Information Systems, Williamsburg, Virginia, United States; William & Mary, Raymond A. Mason School of Business, Williamsburg, Virginia, 23187-8795, United States; University of Virginia McIntire School of Commerce, TI, Charlottesville, Virginia, 22903, United States; Memorial University of Newfoundland, Faculty of Business Administration, St. John's, A1B 3X5, Canada; Georgia State University, Computer Information Systems Department, Atlanta, Georgia, United States
abstract: Machine-learning-based artificial intelligence (AI) systems often perform well in controlled settings but fail when deployed in the real world. These failures stem from a fundamental problem: ML/AI models optimize data-model fit by increasing statistical performance on training data, whereas real-world deployment demands a new paradigm in ML/AI: model-world fit that preserves domain semantics and contextual understanding. We propose a Machine Learning Model-World Fit framework that provides both a conceptual structure for understanding how domain knowledge shapes ML/AI systems and a research roadmap for investigating these relationships. The framework identifies how domain knowledge can be integrated into ML/AI development process via external knowledge representations, such as data, value, process models or domain ontologies. Incorporating external knowledge representations can help overcome three types of knowledge deficiencies in AI: know-what, know-how, and know-why. To illustrate the framework, we apply it to a child welfare placement case, a domain where contextual understanding is critical and statistical accuracy is an insufficient evaluation criterion. Our insights lead to several directions for scholars working at the intersection of machine learning, design science, and knowledge representation.

title: Passing on Talent: A Generativity Perspective on the Effects of Perceived Overqualification Among Older Employees
authors: Jia Yu; Deshani B. Ganegoda; Chao Ma
affiliations: China State Shipbuilding Corporation Limited; Renmin University of China; Melbourne Business School, The University of Melbourne; Xi’an Jiaotong University
abstract: Drawing on generativity theory, we examine the positive effects of perceived overqualification among older employees. Specifically, we argue that perceptions of overqualification in older employees are positively associated with a core generativity motive—that is, a desire to support and guide the next generation and be needed by them. Further, we argue that generativity motive predicts prosocial attitudes and behaviors in the form of prosocial meaning of work for future generations and helping behavior. Additionally, we identify mature-age practices—that is, human resource practices tailored to address older employees’ needs—as a key contextual factor that strengthens the indirect pathway between perceptions of overqualification in older employees and their prosocial attitudes and behaviors. We test and find support for our hypotheses in two independent field studies—a three-wave field study of older employees (Study 1, N = 261) and a dyadic three-wave field study of employees of various ages and their respective supervisors (Study 2, N = 274 dyads). Theoretical and practical implications of our study are discussed.

title: Beyond Good and Bad: Understanding the Contradictory Effects of Positive Leadership Behavior and Negative Leadership Behavior
authors: Haoying (Howie) Xu; Xing Wang; Daan van Knippenberg
affiliations: Stevens Institute of Technology; Colorado State University; Rice University
abstract: Organizational scholarship has long focused on leadership behavior, largely assuming that “good” and “bad” leaders can be distinguished by distinct sets of behaviors that can be organized into constructs with an inherent positive or negative valence (e.g., transformational, ethical, abusive). This assumption has guided extensive construct development and generated a substantial body of evidence consistent with each leadership construct’s expected valence. Yet, emerging research has documented the “dark side” of positive leadership and the “bright side” of negative leadership, revealing effects that contradict these expectations—effects that we call leadership contradictory effects. Despite growing interest in this line of research, the literature remains fragmented, with limited clarity regarding its scope and little theoretical integration explaining why, how, and when such effects occur. This motivates our review, which synthesizes these fragmented findings into a cohesive theoretical account organized around shared themes that cut across leadership constructs. First, we define leadership contradictory effects and review major approaches to operationalize them. Then, we advance an integrative framework that delineates three major theoretical themes, their associated theories, and three categories of boundary conditions to explain why, how, and when leadership contradictory effects arise. Finally, we propose paths forward, including suggestions to guide future research in this emerging domain. Overall, our work reorients scholars and points them beyond valence-based assumptions about leadership effects as a means to explore a broader range of consequences.

title: Mapping Global and Regional Risks: Structural Insights From Systems Thinking and Interpretive Structural Modeling
authors: Abroon Qazi; Fazeelat Aziz
affiliations: School of Business Administration American University of Sharjah Sharjah UAE; College of Economics and Management Shandong University of Science and Technology Qingdao China
abstract: ABSTRACT This study contributes to global risk analysis by providing a structural and exploratory enhancement to the analytical framework used to interpret the World Economic Forum's Global Risks Report (GRR), particularly the 2024 edition. It explores the complex interactions among critical global and regional risks using interpretive structural modeling (ISM) and systems thinking (ST)‐based causal loop diagrams (CLDs). Rather than offering validated intervention guidance or predictive modeling, the study focuses on qualitative and structural mapping of risk interdependencies. Instead of combining the two methodologies, their insights are systematically integrated to provide a deeper understanding of global and regional risk dynamics. Through ISM, the research identifies hierarchical relationships among risks, highlighting key drivers and consequences, while CLDs reveal reinforcing feedback loops and interdependencies that illustrate the cyclical nature of systemic risks. Key findings highlight the critical roles of “extreme weather events,” “pollution,” and “critical change to Earth systems” in global risk networks, and regional dynamics such as “geoeconomic confrontation” and “technological power concentration” in the Middle East. The complementary use of ISM and CLDs offers exploratory insights beyond existing GRR network metrics by making explicit the hierarchical positioning of risks and their qualitative feedback structures. This study positions its contribution as groundwork for future quantitative modeling and scenario analysis, providing interpretive and structural insights rather than operational decision support.

title: When small costs make big impacts: Vertical contracts with menu costs
authors: Ciwei Dong; Xi Li; Xiutian Shi
affiliations: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law; University of Hong Kong; Nanjing University of Science and Technology
abstract: Retailers incur price-adjustment costs called menu costs when changing the prices of their products over time. These products are often sourced from upstream suppliers, who endogenously determine wholesale prices, which have cascading effects on retail prices. In this paper, we consider the pricing strategies of supply chain members in the presence of menu costs. Our analysis suggests that even a minuscule menu cost can substantially affect pricing strategies and the equilibrium outcome. Upstream manufacturers always benefit from a menu cost whereas downstream retailers benefit from only a moderate menu cost and are hurt by both high and low menu costs. Meanwhile, menu costs always alleviate the issue of double marginalization, thereby improving supply chain profits, consumer surplus, and social welfare. This study provides channel members with guidance on how to set prices in the presence of menu costs. It also recommends retailers to optimally maintain a moderate menu cost.

title: How Third‐Party Sellers Respond to Platform Owner Entry: Reselling Versus Private‐Label Modes in E‐Commerce
authors: Shiying Zheng; Xiaodie Pu; Alain Yee Loong Chong
affiliations: Nottingham University Business School China The University of Nottingham Ningbo China Ningbo China
abstract: ABSTRACT E‐commerce platforms depend on a large base of third‐party sellers, yet platform owners increasingly enter the product markets of those sellers, competing with them while retaining control over the search rankings and recommendation systems that shape which products buyers encounter. Prior research on this phenomenon has produced mixed findings and has largely focused on innovation platforms (e.g., app stores and software ecosystems), leaving e‐commerce marketplaces comparatively underexplored. This study examines how third‐party sellers respond to two distinct modes of platform owner entry—reselling, in which the owner begins selling an existing product on the same product listing, and private‐label entry, in which the owner introduces a separately listed substitute whose exposure is also shaped by platform‐controlled search and recommendations. Using longitudinal data from Amazon.com and discontinuous growth modelling, we find that sellers immediately reduce prices following reselling entry but increase prices following private‐label entry. Over the longer term, both entry modes attenuate the trajectories of seller participation and investment in FBA relative to their pre‐entry trajectories, with stronger attenuation following private‐label entry. These findings extend research on platform owner entry by showing that third‐party seller responses vary systematically across entry modes, moving beyond treatments of owner entry as a single competitive event. They also develop a visibility‐based explanation for why seller responses differ across entry modes and show that pricing, participation and platform‐specific investment may unfold over different time horizons following platform owner entry.

title: The Relational Dynamics of Multiparty Alliances: An Interdependence‐Based View
authors: Wenqian Wang; Jiabei Hu; Fabrice Lumineau
affiliations: Hong Kong Baptist University; Purdue University; The University of Hong Kong
abstract: Abstract Despite the increasing relevance of multiparty alliances, existing research remains fragmented and predominantly organized around functional purposes or structural forms, overlooking the relational dynamics among alliance partners. Such an omission prevents a systematic understanding of what fundamentally distinguishes multiparty alliances from their dyadic counterparts and how different types of multiparty alliances vary from one another. This paper addresses this gap through a systematic review of research from leading management journals published between 1990 and 2025. Adopting an interdependence‐based view, we offer two main insights. First, the presence of more than two partners introduces three categorically distinct features compared to dyadic alliances: a change in membership, a change in reciprocity patterns, and the emergence of faultlines. Each of these features poses distinct challenges. Second, and more importantly, we show how pooled, sequential, and reciprocal forms of interdependence shape the emergence, evolution, and consequences of these relational features, thereby explaining systematic variations across multiparty alliances. Building on these insights, we develop an integrative framework that clarifies the distinctiveness of multiparty alliances and identifies key mechanisms and boundary conditions. This framework informs a future research agenda to redirect scholarly attention to the unique relational dynamics within and across multiparty alliances.

title: Is the Gene‐ie Out of the Bottle? The Problems and Perils of Genetics Research in Management
authors: Jean Clarke; Joep Cornelissen; Mark P. Healey
affiliations: emlyon business school; Erasmus University Rotterdam; University of Manchester
abstract: Abstract In recent years, the field of management research has witnessed the emergence of a stream of research that seeks to identify the genetic determinants of managerial, entrepreneurial, and organizational behaviour. We challenge the reductionist epistemology underpinning this genetic perspective in management research and highlight the inherently weak inferences about human behaviour that follow from its prevailing methods and explanatory models. We further examine the ethical implications that arise from its underlying assumptions and potential future applications. We then propose recasting the role of genetics as part of a broader phenomenon‐driven approach towards studying and explaining human behaviour in management research and outline a conceptual framework aimed at generating stronger and contextually grounded explanatory models of managerial, entrepreneurial, and organizational behaviour.

title: Managing Procurement Auction Failure: Bid Requirements or Reserve Prices?
authors: Jun Ma; Vadim Marmer; Pai Xu
affiliations: School of Economics Renmin University of China Beijing China; Vancouver School of Economics University of British Columbia Vancouver Canada; Business School University of Hong Kong Hong Kong China
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines bid requirements, where the government may cancel a procurement contract unless two or more bids are received. Using a first‐price auction model with endogenous entry, we compare the bid requirement and reserve price mechanisms in terms of auction failure and procurement costs. We find that, in comparison with bid requirements, reserve prices can reduce procurement costs and substantially lower failure probabilities, especially when entry costs are high or signals are sufficiently informative. Bid requirements are more likely to result in zero entry, while reserve prices can sustain positive entry under broader conditions.

title: What Explains Growing Gender and Racial Education Gaps?
authors: Zvi Eckstein; Michael Keane; Osnat Lifshitz
affiliations: Reichman University Herzliya Israel; Johns Hopkins University Baltimore Maryland USA; University of New South Wales Sydney Australia
abstract: ABSTRACT We study why US college graduation gaps by gender and race widened across cohorts. We develop a dynamic life‐cycle model with endogenous education, labor supply, marriage, fertility, and welfare participation. Preferences are fixed across cohorts and race/ethnic groups; changes arise from family background, labor‐market opportunities, and marriage markets. Labor‐market changes account for half of growth in women's graduation from the 1960 to 1980 cohorts. Parental background accounts for one quarter and marriage markets for one fifth. These shares are similar for Whites, Blacks, and Hispanics, but absolute gains were larger for White women, which led to wider racial gaps.
